contributions.headingText: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by café-au-lait spots, axillary and inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules of the iris, multiple neurofibromas, and an increased risk for various malignancies.
NF1-related features usually develop in neural crest–derived cells such as Schwann cells, melanocytes, glial cells, adrenal cells, and interstitial cells of Cajal.

Typical manifestations include multiple café-au-lait spots, axillary/inguinal freckling, Lisch nodules, and optic pathway gliomas {28230061}. Café-au-lait spots, the hallmark of NF1, may be present at birth and develop further during the first few years of life. Lisch nodules are asymptomatic iris hamartomas easily detected by slit-lamp examination. Bone abnormalities can cause serious complications in individuals with NF1. Severe scoliosis, sphenoid wing dysplasia, non-ossifying fibromas, and congenital tibial bowing are skeletal abnormalities associated with NF1 {18248783}. Other clinical signs are short stature, macrocephaly, and deficits in attention and cognitive function. Less common complications include epilepsy and cardiovascular problems.

Neoplastic disease spectrum

Children (aged < 5 years) with NF1 have a higher risk of developing juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia than children without NF1, although the annual incidence is low (1 case per 2000–5000 people) {9180088}. Individuals with NF1 are at increased risk of developing benign and malignant solid tumours of both nervous and non-nervous systems {19410195}. In children with café-au-lait macules and malignant tumours, constitutional mismatch repair deficiency syndrome should be considered in the differential diagnosis {30415209}.

Non–nervous system tumours

An association between digital glomus tumours and NF1 has been described {20530151}. Children with NF1 may develop non-ossifying fibromas of the long bones, sometimes reported as Jaffe–Campanacci syndrome {24232412}. Individuals with NF1 have a lifetime risk as high as 6% of developing gastrointestinal stromal tumours {26511941}, which mostly affect the small intestine and are multifocal {16330947}. Systematic screening in a cohort of adults with NF1 detects phaeochromocytoma in > 5% {27460956; 27450695}. Women with NF1 have an increased risk of developing breast cancer before the age of 50 years, and systematic screening is recommended starting from the age of 30 years {28860858; 26926675}. Somatostatinomas (duodenal carcinoids) are rarely detected and are often metastatic when diagnosed {20300877}.

Peripheral nervous system tumours

Multiple cutaneous neurofibromas are benign peripheral nerve sheath tumours that typically develop starting at puberty and are present in > 90% of adults with NF1 {28230061}. In contrast, studies suggest that plexiform neurofibromas are of congenital origin and occur in 30–50% of individuals with NF1 {28230061}. Cutaneous neurofibromas are typically benign, whereas plexiform neurofibromas have a risk of becoming malignant. Individuals with NF1 have a 9–15% lifetime risk of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST) development {26926675; 23036231}. Individuals with a germline NF1 microdeletion have an at least 2 times increased risk of developing MPNSTs {12660952}.

CNS tumours

Tumours of the optic pathway occur in 15% of children with NF1 {28806346}. Only one third of children with optic pathway gliomas develop symptoms such as visual impairment. Most NF1-associated brain tumours in children are classified as pilocytic astrocytoma WHO grade 1. Brain tumours in adults with NF1 are less common and have a higher malignant potential {30531922}.
NF1 is an autosomal dominant disorder with a birth incidence of 1 case per 2000–3500 people {25354145; 28230061}.

NF1 is caused by inactivating mutations in the NF1 gene, mapping to chromosome band 17q11.2, that encodes neurofibromin (NF1) {2134734; 2114220; 1694727}. Neurofibromin (NF1) is expressed widely during embryonic development but most abundantly in the CNS. Neurofibromin (NF1) is expressed in Schwann cells, melanocytes, neurons and oligodendrocytes, leukocytes, adrenal medulla, and many other cell types. Half of the subjects with NF1 have a de novo mutation in the NF1 gene.

Neurofibromin (NF1) acts as a tumour suppressor {8499945; 25877329}. Different interaction partners of neurofibromin (NF1) have been described, but the most important functional domain is the RAS-GAP–related domain. Neurofibromin (NF1) is a negative regulator of the RAS/MAPK pathway and stimulates the intrinsic GTPase activity of RAS, resulting in the conversion of RAS-GTP into inactive RAS-GDP {25877329}. SPRED1 (the protein implicated in Legius syndrome) binds to neurofibromin (NF1) on both sides of the GAP-related domain and recruits neurofibromin (NF1) to the membrane where it can downregulate RAS-GTP {22751498; 26635368; 27313208}.

A second hit in NF1 has been reported in associated tumours such as MPNSTs, neurofibromas, neuroblastomas, astrocytomas, gastrointestinal stromal tumours, optic pathway glioma, phaeochromocytomas, glomus tumours, juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia, and breast cancer {19410195; 29926297}. A second hit has also been reported in non-tumoural manifestations such as café-au-lait spots {17914445} and pseudarthrosis tissue {16773574; 25612910}. The heterozygous NF1 background in non-tumoural cells such as mast cells plays a role in oncogenesis in mouse models of NF1 {18984156}.
The tumours are histopathologically identical to their sporadic counterparts.

A pathogenic NF1 mutation can be detected in as many as 95% of individuals with NF1 {10862084}. In 5% of cases, an NF1 microdeletion has been identified {28213670}. Individuals with an NF1 microdeletion co-deleting the SUZ12 gene have an increased risk of developing MPNST {12660952}. SUZ12 codes for a component of PRC2, which has been implicated in MPNST development {25119042; 25240281; 25305755}. Women with NF1 microdeletions are underrepresented in the group of women with NF1 and breast cancer {30530636}. A few other genotype–phenotype correlations have been reported. Individuals with NF1 with a specific 3 bp deletion (c.2970_2972del) or a missense mutation affecting p.Arg1809 do not show neurofibromas or other NF1-associated tumours and the disorder cannot be differentiated clinically from Legius syndrome {30190611; 26178382; 25370043; 17160901}. Individuals with NF1 missense mutations affecting codons 844–848 have a higher incidence of externally visible plexiform neurofibromas, symptomatic spinal neurofibromas, optic pathway glioma, and MPNST compared with the general NF1 population {29290338}. In cases of mosaicism for the NF1 mutation, it is frequently not possible to detect the responsible postzygotic NF1 mutation in peripheral white blood cells, and the NF1 mutation can be identified only in purified cells from affected tissues {17668375}.

Diagnostic criteria for NF1 were established during a consensus conference of the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) {3128965}. Patients must exhibit two or more of the following features: ≥ 6 café-au-lait spots (> 5 mm in diameter in children, > 15 mm in adults), ≥ 2 cutaneous or subcutaneous neurofibromas or 1 plexiform neurofibroma, axillary/inguinal freckling, optic pathway glioma, ≥ 2 Lisch nodules in the iris, bone dysplasia, a first-degree relative with NF1 (by the above criteria). In the revised criteria (not yet published at the time this text was prepared) a pathogenic NF1 mutation will be part of the criteria.
Individuals with NF1 have an increased standardized mortality ratio of 3.22 (2.81–3.68) mainly resulting from malignancy and cardiovascular problems {25354145}.
